subject: analysing aerial survey data in distance

messages.author: 209d308734be2077
messages.subject: analysing aerial survey data in distance
parts:
Hi All,



We are trialling an aerial survey technique for seabird surveys across the
ocean.



I have looked at Distance to analyse the data but I am having issues
preparing the data to input, and understanding some of the terminology.



Our survey was conducted at 80m altitude, 80kts speed and we divided the
survey area in to various zones (A,B,C) representing distance from aircraft.



We estimate a 40m band below the aircraft that we cannot survey.



Transects were 60 km long, separated by 2km and there were 21 Transects.



We recorded multi species data, inputted in Excel. This includes individual
sightings and flocks.



Is there anyone out there who could assist in advising on how to input data
into distance and what we should watch out for?



Thanks

Chris

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: analysing aerial survey data in distance
parts:
Chris:

You have a good start on organising your data for analysis. The
terminology of the way your data were collected is "binned" data, in
that you have distance bands in which your sightings were made rather
than exact distances to the centres of the detected flocks.

I take it from your flight altitude, you know the perpendicular distance
from the flight line to the edges of your three distance bands. You
will enter the perpendicular distance for detections in Band A as the
average of the perpendicular distances from the two edges of band A (40m
and the outer edge). You will do the same for the other two bands.
There is a sample Distance project (distributed with the software)
"Ducknest" that shows how binned data are entered.

You can enter all the data from your survey into a single Distance
project, recording the species of birds detected in the "observation
layer" along with the distance band and the size of the cluster
(flock). You can use the filtering capacity in Distance to analyse
species individually by filtering for observations of "species x".

The other issue for you is the unobservable strip under the plane.
Methods for dealing with this are discussed in Section 7.6.1 of Buckland
et al. (2001) "Introduction to Distance sampling".

One of the challenges of analysing seabird data is their spatial
clustering; some transects may have many flocks, other transects may
have very few (or zero) flocks. That will make variability between
transects quite high. But that issue will only become apparent after
you have gotten your data into Distance and begun some exploratory analyses.

If you have further questions, feel free to contact me off list.
